Under the simple “evenly distributed over four spacelike dimensions” assumption, and if our ordinary world accesses only **three of those four spatial degrees of freedom**, then the crude fraction accessible is:

\[
\frac{3}{4}=75\%
\]

So the inaccessible fraction would be:

\[
\frac{1}{4}=25\%
\]

That would give a dark/inaccessible component of roughly **25%** of the expansion energy.

But there’s a sharper geometric caveat: if the fourth spatial dimension is continuous and our 3D slice has literally zero thickness in that direction, then a perfect 3D slice intersects a 4D volume in a measure-zero way. In that case, the accessible fraction is not 75%; it is effectively **zero unless there is coupling, projection, leakage, brane thickness, or some intersection rule**.

So the answer depends on the model:

In a **degree-of-freedom bookkeeping** model: about **25% inaccessible**.

In a **literal 3D hyperslice through 4D volume** model: almost **all of it is inaccessible by normal 3D observation**, unless the fourth-dimensional energy projects into our slice gravitationally or through some field coupling.

[L690] In a word, the feeling of
[L691] mathematical elegance is only the satisfaction due to any adaptation of
[L692] the solution to the needs of our mind, and it is because of this very
[L693] adaptation that this solution can be for us an instrument. Consequently
[L694] this esthetic satisfaction is bound up with the economy of thought.
[L695] Again the comparison of the Erechtheum comes to my mind, but I must not
[L696] use it too often.
[L697]
[L698] It is for the same reason that, when a rather long calculation has led
[L699] to some simple and striking result, we are not satisfied until we have
[L700] shown that we should have been _able to foresee_, if not this entire
[L701] result, at least its most characteristic traits. Why? What prevents our
[L702] being content with a calculation which has told us, it seems, all we
[L703] wished to know? It is because, in analogous cases, the long calculation
[L704] might not again avail, and that this is not so about the reasoning often
[L705] half intuitive which would have enabled us to foresee. This reasoning
[L706] being short, we see at a single glance all its parts, so that we
[L707] immediately perceive what must be changed to adapt it to all the
[L708] problems of the same nature which can occur. And then it enables us to
[L709] foresee if the solution of these problems will be simple, it shows us at
[L710] least if the calculation is worth undertaking.
[L711]
[L712] What we have just said suffices to show how vain it would be to seek to
[L713] replace by any mechanical procedure the free initiative of the
[L714] mathematician. To obtain a result of real value, it is not enough to
[L715] grind out calculations, or to have a machine to put things in order; it
[L716] is not order alone, it is unexpected order, which is worth while. The
[L717] machine may gnaw on the crude fact, the soul of the fact will always
[L718] escape it.
[L719]
[L720] Since the middle of the last century, mathematicians are more and more
[L721] desirous of attaining absolute rigor; they are right, and this tendency
[L722] will be more and more accentuated. In mathematics rigor is not
[L723] everything, but without it there is nothing. A demonstration which is
[L724] not rigorous is nothingness. I think no one will contest this truth. But
[L725] if it were taken too literally, we should be led to conclude that before
[L726] 1820, for example, there was no mathematics; this would be manifestly
[L727] excessive; the geometers of that time understood voluntarily what we
[L728] explain by prolix discourse. This does not mean that they did not see it
[L729] at all; but they passed over it too rapidly, and to see it well would
[L730] have necessitated taking the pains to say it.
[L731]
[L732] But is it always needful to say it so many times? Those who were the
[L733] first to emphasize exactness before all else have given us arguments
[L734] that we may try to imitate; but if the demonstrations of the future are
[L735] to be built on this model, mathematical treatises will be very long; and
[L736] if I fear the lengthenings, it is not solely because I deprecate
[L737] encumbering libraries, but because I fear that in being lengthened out,
[L738] our demonstrations may lose that appearance of harmony whose usefulness
[L739] I have just explained.
[L740]
[L741] The economy of thought is what we should aim at, so it is not enough to
[L742] supply models for imitation. It is needful for those after us to be able
[L743] to dispense with these models and, in place of repeating an argument
[L744] already made, summarize it in a few words. And this has already been
[L745] attained at times. For instance, there was a type of reasoning found
[L746] everywhere, and everywhere alike. They were perfectly exact but long.
